name: LCROSS
intro: LCROSS was the shepherding spacecraft that steered the Centaur rocket stage to the Moon. It let go 10 hours before impact, followed behind, flew through the Centaur’s plume measuring everything, then crashed into Cabeus crater too, about four minutes later.
whyLeft: Its whole mission was planned so that its most important science happened in the last four minutes, ending in its own crash.
repurpose: Its crater is a second dig into the same icy floor, a ready-made target for a future rover with lights to study the ice up close.
funFact: LCROSS radioed all its plume measurements home live, because it knew it would be destroyed minutes later.

hotspots.title: Second crater
hotspots.text: LCROSS hit here at 11:35 UT, just over four minutes after the Centaur and a few kilometres away, in the same permanently dark crater floor.

hotspots.title: Last view
hotspots.text: On the way down, LCROSS’s cameras watched the target area. It carried two visible-light cameras, three infrared cameras, three spectrometers and a light meter.

photo.alt: A grainy view of the dark lunar south polar region from the LCROSS spacecraft
photo.caption: The Centaur’s target area in Cabeus, seen by LCROSS’s visible camera during its final approach.

hotspots.title: Through the plume
hotspots.text: LCROSS flew straight through the dust cloud kicked up by the Centaur, sniffing it with its spectrometers. That is how scientists found water in the plume.

source.label: Colaprete et al. (NASA Ames), Science 2010: water in the LCROSS plume

hotspots.title: Built on a ring
hotspots.text: LCROSS was built around a ring normally used to hold small satellites on a rocket, 1.58 m wide. Scout, look for twisted pieces of that ring; they are all that might remain.
